reading.body:
Education AI is tracked here through policy, market intelligence, and course listings, not through specific tools or infrastructure.

The four entries point to federal guidance for schools, a market-intelligence platform covering EdTech funding and AI learning platforms, and two references to a catalog of courses and credentials. The summary identifies tutoring systems, drafting assistance, and academic integrity policy as the live questions from K-12 through university. That pattern suggests the field is being defined by rules and training pathways more than by named deployments.

For AI scaling, this data offers no direct signal about compute, buildings, or power. It does not list data centers, energy demand, or hardware. What it does show is that education's AI footprint is currently administrative and pedagogical, with procurement and credentialing as the visible pressure points. Readers should not infer infrastructure constraints from this set.

analysis.body:
Per the Census Bureau, 30.0% of firms in educational services (NAICS 61) answered yes to whether the business had used AI in the last two weeks, against 35.5% in the prior period. The question was first asked in September 2023, so the series is short, and the Census note records that some values are suppressed. That is the only measured adoption figure in the material here, and it counts firms rather than classrooms, students, or institutions.

The Department of Education issued the federal guidance, and its page carries an inventory of the Department's own AI use-cases. Those include CAISY, described as delivering real-time insights, predictive analytics, and intelligent automation to streamline repetitive tasks and improve situational awareness, alongside Grammarly for written communication, Otter.AI for real-time transcription and collaboration, and AWS Bedrock for building and scaling applications powered by foundation models. The listed uses are largely drafting and analysis work: generating summaries and outlines for projects and presentations, producing code snippets in a variety of programming languages, writing R code for data analysis, training employees on prompt engineering, converting between related data types such as a county name and its FIPS code, generating mock data sets for testing, extracting action items from public documents, drafting outreach strategies and project plans, and suggesting descriptive paragraphs, workflow diagrams, and qualifications for public positions. One entry describes feeding fabricated examples of prohibited prompt information to test filters and data loss prevention.

The regulatory posture in that same guidance is framed around adherence to federal regulations on AI advancement, responsible and secure usage, and procurement, with the Department's OCIO supporting compliance in accordance with the Executive Order Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence. The sourced points describe the guidance as framing permissible use, risk, and procurement for US education.

HolonIQ tracks the education economy, describing itself as a platform for impact market intelligence covering EdTech funding, digital transformation, and AI learning platforms across K-12, higher ed, and workforce learning. Its page describes sizing addressable markets, quantifying demand, forecasting scenarios at varying rates of growth, quantifying impact with rubrics, ratings and scoring, and supporting policy, procurement and investment decisions, and it says it serves governments, institutions, technology companies, global firms and investors. The excerpt does not report specific funding totals or adoption rates for education, so nothing more precise can be drawn from it here.

Courses and certifications are catalogued here, with 13 AI courses listed, 11 of them free, and 3 carrying public companion code, curated by level and audience with one verified source each and re-verified daily. The catalog splits between university graduate courses with public materials, Stanford's CS224n and CS231n, UC Berkeley's CS285, and MIT's 6.S191, and industry offerings from DeepLearning.AI, Google, Hugging Face, fast.ai, and independent researcher Andrej Karpathy. The page notes that university courses are generally structured around exam-driven theory while the industry courses are described as code-first or hands-on, and it states plainly that the data does not report enrollment numbers, completion rates, or which course is most widely taken. Membership in the catalog is editorial, based on significance rather than sponsorship.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material supports a few narrow conclusions. Measured firm-level use sits at 30.0% per the Census Bureau, below the prior period's 35.5%, so adoption in this sector is neither universal nor clearly rising on this evidence. The Department of Education's inventory shows where deployment has actually landed in a federal education agency, mostly in drafting, summarization, transcription, code assistance, and internal testing rather than in instruction itself, and its framing ties use to federal regulation, security, and procurement review. The sources here describe intended benefits such as reduced costs and improved productivity but report no measured return on investment, and HolonIQ's page describes market intelligence services rather than results, so any ROI claim would go beyond what these pages say.

https://www.holoniq.com/.brief: HolonIQ describes itself as a platform that supplies data and research on the global impact economy. It offers tools for sizing markets, forecasting growth, and measuring impact through rubrics and ratings. The site also claims to provide competitive intelligence, partnership mapping, and strategic guidance for digital transformation. Users can receive newsletters with trending topics about impact, technology, and finance.

https://www.ed.gov/about/ed-overview/art.brief: The Department of Education's Office of the Chief Information Officer oversees the department's use of artificial intelligence in compliance with federal regulations and an executive order on AI leadership. The department has catalogued multiple AI applications across its operations, including tools for meeting transcription, writing assistance, code generation, data analysis, and document summarization. Additional uses include generating mock datasets for testing, automating data conversions, creating job descriptions, developing outreach strategies, and testing security filters. The guidance reflects the department's approach to balancing AI innovation with responsible and secure deployment.
